File:Acheroraptor reconstruction.jpg.ImageDescription: Reconstruction of Acheroraptor , the new Hell Creek dromaeosaur described by Evans et al. November 2013. It's known only from the maxilla and dentary, so only the head and neck are illustrated. It's depicted staring at a hispine beetle, of which there is abundance evidence (Johnson et al 2000) from Hell Creek ichnofossils. Phylogenetic analysis recovers it as a velociraptorine, the most basal member of the group containing Velociraptor , Adasaurus and Tsaagan .

File:Acheroraptor skull reconstruction.p.ImageDescription: Reconstruction of the skull of Acheroraptor temertyorum, a dromaeosaurid from the Late Cretaceous Hell Creek formation, known material highlighted in white. This particular reconstruction was based on a saurornitholestine position, but it has also been recovered as a velociraptorine. Unknown material filled in using Atrociraptor, Saurornitholestes, and Deinonychus. Total skull length is approximately 23.5 cm from the premaxilla to the quadrate.

File:Albertonykus TD.png.ImageDescription: Albertonykus is the earliest and smallest known alvarezsaurid from North America, reaching about 1 m in total body length. Alvarezsaurids are known for their long skinny legs adapted for running, and extremely reduced forelimbs. Albertonykus supports the theory that alvarezsaurs originated in South America and dispersed to Asia through North America.

File:Bonapartenykus TD.png.ImageDescription: Bonapartenykus is a relatively basal alvarezsauroid dinosaur that lived approximately 71 million years ago in the Late Cretaceous of what is now Argentina. True alvarezsaurs are some of the smallest non-avian dinosaurs, but Bonapartenykus is considerably larger at about 2.5 m in length, and weighing around 70 kg. Though lacking in the fossil record, it is thought that it had the diminshed arms and single large claw that derived alvarezsaurs are known for.

File:Diuqin TD.png.ImageDescription: Diuqin is an unenlagiine dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Argentina. Unenlagiines, known exclusively from South America, are usually classified as dromaeosaurs though this is sometimes debated. Like dromaeosaurs, they were covered in feathers, carnivorous, and had the large sickle-like claw on the inner toe of each foot. Unique to unenlagiines is their elongated snout, suggesting a piscivorous diet. Diuqin was a medium-sized unenlagiine, at about 4 m in length.

File:Duonychus TD.png.ImageDescription: Duonychus preserved the largest keratin hand claw sheaths of any known dinosaur, at 30 cm in length. Large claws are typical for therizinosaurs, but Duonychus only had two fingers per hand, unique among the known therizinosauria. It was herbivorous, likely using these claws to pull branches toward its mouth. Duonychus was about 3 m long in total body length.

File:Eoneophron TD.png.ImageDescription: Eoneophron is a caenagnathid theropod dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous Hell Creek Formation of North America. Caenagnathids can be differentiated from other oviraptorosaurs by their distinct jaws, which tended to be relatively long and shallow, suggesting that the bite was not as powerful. Caenagnathids also tended to be more lightly built. They had slender arms and long, gracile legs, although they didn't seem to be especially cursorial. Eoneophron's body mass is estimated at approximately 78

File:Harenadraco TD.png.ImageDescription: Harenadraco is a small troodontid dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Mongolia. It was small and lightly built, typical for troodontids, but Harenadraco had uniquely slender legs. This adaptation, which allowed for skilled running abilities, implies that it could have hunted highly agile prey. Harenadraco was about 1 m in length, and most likely covered in feathers, which further aided in its agility while running and hunting.

File:Incisivosaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Incisivosaurus is a small basal oviraptorosaur known for its distinctive teeth. While derived members typically lacked teeth entirely, Incisivosaurus had large mammal-like incisors, giving it its name. These unique teeth give insight into the evolution of oviraptorosaurs. Incisivosaurus grew to about 1 m in length, and was likely herbivorous, or possibly omnivorous.

File:Jaculinykus TD.png.ImageDescription: Jaculinykus is a small alvarezsaurid theropod from the Late Cretaceous of what is now Mongolia. The name is a reference to the Jaculus, a small dragon in Greek mythology. Like other Alvarezsaurids, Jaculinykus had long legs, and enlarged first digit claws on each hand, which were probably used for digging and tearing. It also had a long tube-shaped snout filled with tiny teeth. These adaptations indicate that it probably had an insectivorous diet, feeding on colonial insects such as termites.

File:Achillobator TD.png.ImageDescription: Achillobator is a dromaeosaurid dinosaur that lived in Asia during the Late Cretaceous period. It is named in reference to the large Achilles tendon that supported the sickle claw, characteristic to most dromaeosaurs. It was a large, heavy-built, ground-dwelling, bipedal carnivore that would have been an active feathered predator. Reaching up to 5 m in length with a body mass about 250 kg, Achillobator is considered to be one of the largest dromaeosaurs.

File:Kayrasaurus TD.png.ImageDescription: Kayrasaurus is a therizinosaurian dinosaur that lived during the Early Cretaceous period in what is now China. At an estimated 3.6 m in total body length, it is the largest therizinosaur known from the Jehol Biota. Like other therizinosaurs, Kayrasaurus was a bipedal herbivore with large curved claws on each hand.

File:Migmanychion TD.png.ImageDescription: Migmanychion is a genus of small-bodied theropod dinosaur from the Early Cretaceous of China. It is known from a well-articulated left hand, which gives it its name, showing a peculiar combination of features shared with therizinosauroids and oviraptorosaurs. Migmanychion is a maniraptoran theropod, but its precise placement within the clade is unclear. It seems most closely related to Fukuivenator, which is currently thought to be a basal therizinosaur. Migmanychion was roughly 2 m in length.

File:Archaeopteryx TD.png.ImageDescription: Between the late 19th century and the early 21st century, Archaeopteryx was generally accepted by paleontologists as the oldest known bird. Archaeopteryx lived in the Late Jurassic around 150 million years ago, in what is now southern Germany. The largest species could grow to about 0.5 m in length. Despite their small size, broad wings, and inferred ability to fly or glide, Archaeopteryx had more in common with other small Mesozoic dinosaurs than with modern birds.

File:Shuvuuia TD.png.ImageDescription: Shuvuuia is a small, bird-like theropod in the family Alvarezsauridae. It is one of the smallest known non-avian dinosaurs, at just 1 m in length and weighing about 3.5 kg. Shuvuuia had a fragile skull, long legs for running, and short powerful arms with a large claw on each hand. Like all alvarezsaurids, it is thought that the small but robust arms were adapted for digging and tearing. This, along with the long tube-like snout suggest that Shuvuuia fed on colonial insects like termites. Shuvuui

File:Yi TD.png.ImageDescription: Yi is a small derived theropod dinosaur that seems to have evolved wings independently of the traditional bird lineage. Though densely feathered, these wings are made up of a thin membrane stretched between elongated fingers, and a distinctive structure extending from the wrist. Whether these strange wings were capable of flight remains unknown.

File:Yuanyanglong TD.png.ImageDescription: Yuanyanglong is a basal oviraptorosaur with long enigmatic legs. It seems to have had a wading lifestyle, but its short snout does not support an aquatic diet. Another theory is that Yuanyanglong may have been specialized for running, but the structure of its hips are less than ideal. Associated gastroliths suggest it may have had an herbivorous or omnivorous diet.

File:Yulong TD.png.ImageDescription: Yulong is a derived oviraptorid dinosaur known from many well-preserved juvenile individuals, representing some of the smallest known oviraptorids in the fossil record. It was bipedal and feathered, and likely omnivorous or herbivorous. Though known mainly from immature individuals, adult Yulong likely didn't exceed 1 m in total body length.

The holotype UMNH VP 20211 consists of cervical, dorsal and caudal vertebrae. File:Infernogallus TD.png.ImageDescription: Infernogallus is an oviraptorosaurian theropod dinosaur from the Hell Creek formation of what is now North America. Small for a caenagnathid, it grew to approximately 1.5 m in body length and weighed an estimated 12 kg. Infernogallus is the first caenagnathid discovered with a nearly complete skull, which reveals it likely had a frugivorous, or fruit-eating diet.

File:Dinevenator TD.png.ImageDescription: Dinevenator is a derived troodontid dinosaur notable for being relatively robust in terms of its paravian relatives. Like all troodontids, it was covered in feathers, and had a sickle-shaped toe claw on each foot, similar to the one seen in dromaeosaurs. Dinevenator was a small dinosaur, at about 2 m in total body length.

File:Kank TD.png.ImageDescription: Kank is an unenlagiid theropod dinosaur that grew to around 2 meters in total body length. Like all unenlagiids, it was feathered, long-legged, with a longer snout than its close dromaeosaur relatives. Its discovery bridges the geographic gap of unenlagiid dinosaurs between South America and Antarctica.

File:Manipulonyx TD.png.ImageDescription: Manipulonyx is an alvarezsaurid theropod whose discovery revealed this family may be adapted toward an egg-based diet. Smaller claws on the hands prove mechanically capable of holding an egg in place, while a larger claw would puncture the shell. This hypothesis questions the previously standing idea that alvarezsaurs were specially adapted to insectivory.

File:Davide Bonadonna Nemegt Formation.p.ImageDescription: Figure 3. Dinosaur ecology in the Nemegt Basin (Upper Cretaceous of Mongolia). A Tarbosaurus is consuming a Deinocheirus carcass, imposing a distortive, first-order taphonomic filter for interpreting the palaeoecology of this community (the hadrosaurid Saurolophus drinking opposite the tyrannosaurid and the sauropod Nemegtosaurus foraging in the background). Reconstruction by Davide Bonadonna.

File:Fujianvenator TD.png.ImageDescription: Fujianvenator is an anchiornithid avialan from the Late Jurassic of China, whose discovery gave important insight to the evolution of birds. It had proportionately long legs, with the tibia twice the length of the femur. This suggests it may have been a strong runner, and possibly had a terrestrial or wading lifestyle. Fujianvenator was a small dinosaur, weighing about 640 g. As an avialan, it was almost certainly covered in feathers, though it does not seem likely to have been capable of flight
